extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and writers interested in experimental French fiction (Nouveau Roman)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for composing fiction in the Nouveau Roman tradition: experimental novels that break with conventional chronology, plot, character, and narration, emphasize objects and precise description, and often engage with theoretical and cinematic approaches. Useful for writers seeking to emulate or study this mid-20th-century French movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with style
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers 'experimented with style in each novel, creating an essentially new style each time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each novel should explore new formal and stylistic approaches rather than repeating an established technique; the movement prized variety and formal reinvention. Examples on the page include Robbe-Grillet, Butor, and Sarraute. Anti-pattern: producing successive works that reuse the same conventional novelistic techniques without innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of traditional chronology, plot, character, and omniscient narration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nouveau Roman 'generally rejected the traditional use of chronology, plot, character, and the omniscient narrator in fiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on linear chronology, conventional plot arcs, psychologically rounded characters, or an all-knowing narrator to carry the work. Instead, break chronology, fragment or deprioritize plot, present characters indirectly, and avoid authoritative omniscience. Anti-pattern: restoring conventional narrative comforts (clear plot progression, authoritative narrator) undermines the movement's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on objects and detailed description
rubrics_metrics.description: Robbe-Grillet proposed a theory in which the ideal nouveau roman 'would be an individual version and vision of things, subordinating plot and character to the details of the world'—i.e., a novel focused on objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize careful, often repetitive or precise description of objects, settings, and material details. Let these descriptions drive texture and meaning rather than serving only as background for action or psychology. Example novels cited (for their attention to objects/details): La Jalousie, La Modification. Anti-pattern: using object descriptions purely as ornament or as mere supports for conventional plot development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of plot and character to perception/description
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot and character should be subordinated to the writer's depiction of the world and to modes of perception rather than being central organizing principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape narrative emphasis around perception, observation, and descriptive patterning. Character 'development' may instead emerge as a function of how the world is observed and recorded. Scoring note: works are judged by the coherence and originality of their observational approach more than by traditional character arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of an individual 'version' or vision in each work
rubrics_metrics.description: Each novel is expected to present 'an individual version and vision of things'—a singular, self-contained way of seeing or structuring reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each book as a distinct experiment with its own organizing principle or worldview. Avoid serially applying the same 'voice' or organizing gimmick across works; instead aim for a distinct conceptual/formal project per novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical self-consciousness and critical writing about practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouveau Roman authors wrote theoretical essays (e.g., Nathalie Sarraute's L'Ère du soupçon; Robbe-Grillet and Butor's essays) that articulated aims and methods for their fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position fiction in relation to explicit theoretical concerns: consider writing critical or programmatic texts alongside fiction, or ensure the fiction reflects a clear set of aesthetic principles. Works influenced by explicit manifestos or essays are typical; anti-pattern: claiming adherence to the movement while producing conventional narratives without theoretical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cinematic influence and filmic techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nouveau Roman style 'left its mark on the screen' and authors were influenced by cinema (Left Bank, French New Wave), with collaborations producing films like Hiroshima mon amour and Last Year at Marienbad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate filmic techniques—fragmentation, montage-like sequencing, visual attention to surfaces, elliptical time, and spatial choreography—into prose. Consider cinematic pacing and visual composition as organizational strategies for the novel. Example anti-pattern: purely theatrical or stage-bound prose that ignores cinematic sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to diverse literary influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors were 'open to influences from writers such as Dostoevsky, Joyce, Faulkner and Kafka, as well as the cinema.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on a wide range of literary and artistic models to inform formal experiments; synthesize influences rather than imitating a single predecessor. Use intertextual awareness to enrich formal innovation. Anti-pattern: narrow imitation of one antecedent without formally integrating varied influences.
